issue: Joint CAI/OPC/BC/Alberta investigation into whether ChatGPT's training and deployment (GPT-3.5/4) complied with privacy law on collection, consent, transparency, accuracy, retention, and privacy-by-default.
outcome: CAI found OpenAI's initial training-data collection overbroad and non-compliant with Quebec's Private Sector Act (arts. 8 and 9.1); four recommendations issued on consent notices, opt-out-by-default training use, privacy-by-default settings, and retention transparency.
notes: Joint investigation; the federal OPC published the joint findings report. No monetary penalty imposed: recommendations only.

issue: Joint investigation (CAI, OPC, BC and Alberta commissioners) into TikTok's collection and use of minors' personal information.
outcome: Joint investigation conclusions published; findings on minors' data practices announced at a joint press conference.
notes: CAI page links to the federal OPC communiqué and joint findings report. No monetary penalty imposed.

issue: Use of dashcam video surveillance filming the inside of delivery-truck cabs, recording continuously over 14-day periods.
outcome: Ordered to limit in-cab collection to a few seconds around incidents, stop recording after engine shutdown, destroy excess footage, and restrict access to footage to serious accidents/incidents.
notes: Decision rendered 2025-05-20 (dossier 1031833-S); announced by the CAI on 2025-05-28.

issue: Planned facial-recognition pilot (Metro, Super C, Jean Coutu banners) to identify people previously involved in shoplifting or fraud, requiring a biometric characteristics bank.
outcome: Prohibited from putting the biometric bank into service: identity verification via biometrics requires express consent, which was not obtained. First order under s.45 of the Act respecting the legal framework for information technology.
notes: CAI announced the decision on 2025-02-27; the communiqué describes the decision as 'recently rendered', so the decision date may slightly precede this date.

issue: Facial-recognition system used to control employee access to premises; biometric data bank created during COVID-19 temperature-screening era and kept afterwards.
outcome: Ordered within 90 days to stop collecting employees' facial biometrics, stop using facial recognition for access control, and destroy existing biometric templates and encoded representations.
notes: CAI's 10th biometrics decision since 2000. Company had notified the CAI of the biometric bank on 2020-10-02.

issue: Commissioner-initiated investigation into whether Grok (X Corp./xAI) obtained valid consent to collect, use and disclose personal information of identifiable individuals to generate sexually explicit deepfakes, and whether that purpose was appropriate under PIPEDA.
outcome: Well-founded and not resolved at report date: no valid consent obtained for the collection, use and disclosure; a reasonable person would consider the purpose inappropriate; respondents' safeguards judged insufficient to demonstrate effectiveness. Recommendations issued; OPC will continue monitoring.
notes: Commissioner-initiated complaints under PIPEDA s.11(2), Jan 2026; single report covering both respondents. No monetary penalty under PIPEDA; recommendations only.

issue: Investigation into Loblaw's retention of PC Optimum loyalty members' purchase history after account deletion, and whether removing direct identifiers was sufficient to consider the data anonymized.
outcome: Well-founded and conditionally resolved: Loblaw took an unreasonable time to handle deletion and privacy requests (contravening Principle 4.10) and did not demonstrate retained data was properly anonymized (Principle 4.5). Agreed to an independent third-party review of its anonymization process.
notes: Covers complaints received from May 2024 onward. No monetary penalty under PIPEDA; recommendations only.

issue: Whether returned laptops resold through Staples' Openbox program were adequately wiped of previous customers' personal information before resale, and whether staff procedures and training were adequate.
outcome: Well-founded and conditionally resolved: procedures and training inadequate, contravening Principles 4.7.1 and 4.7.3. Staples agreed to clear wipe procedures aligned with manufacturer guidelines, staff training, and annual independent third-party spot checks of stores for 3 years.
notes: Follows a 2011 OPC audit that also found Staples' wipe procedures inadequate. No monetary penalty under PIPEDA; recommendations only.

issue: Privately owned swimming pool required parents to accept a waiver allowing photos/videos of their children to be taken and posted publicly for promotional purposes as a condition of enrolling in swimming lessons.
outcome: Well-founded and resolved: requiring consent for promotional photos as a condition of service contravened Principles 4.3.3 and 4.3.6; the respondent agreed to implement an opt-in photo policy within 4 months.
notes: OPC does not name the respondent; described only as a privately-run swimming pool in Canada. No monetary penalty under PIPEDA; recommendations only.

issue: Complaint that Google's search engine returned outdated media articles about a complainant (a stayed HIV non-disclosure criminal charge) when their name was searched, causing significant harm; whether PIPEDA requires de-listing.
outcome: Well-founded (and unresolved): continued display contravened subsection 5(3) of PIPEDA; OPC recommended Google de-list the articles from name searches. Google declined, saying courts should decide whether PIPEDA includes a right to de-list.
notes: Complaint dates to 2017; Federal Court (2021) and Federal Court of Appeal (2023) confirmed PIPEDA applies to Google's search service. No monetary penalty under PIPEDA; recommendations only.

issue: Appeal of the CAI's December 2021 order against Clearview AI's mass scraping of images from websites and social media to build a facial-recognition database, without consent and without a serious and legitimate interest.
outcome: Cour du Québec rejected Clearview AI's appeal grounds and confirmed the December 2021 order requiring it to stop collecting Quebecers' personal information and destroy their images and biometric identifiers; the court found a real and substantial connection between Clearview AI and Quebec, and held the consent requirements did not unjustly limit freedom of expression.
notes: Cour du Québec judgment confirming the CAI's December 2021 order; the CAI announced the outcome on 2026-10-16. Court decision, not a new CAI order. The court did not rule on the applicability of the order, treating it as a question of fact.

issue: Residential property manager collected social insurance numbers (SINs) and copies of driver's licences from two prospective lease assignees, and refused their lease-assignment applications for not providing them; the company also lacked published privacy-governance policies and a named privacy officer.
outcome: Ordered to stop collecting SINs from prospective tenants or assignees without a specific justification (name, first name, address and date of birth suffice for a credit check); stop refusing applicants for not providing unnecessary personal information, including driver's licence copies; redact or destroy SIN documents collected without justification within 30 days; establish and implement personal-information governance policies and publish them in plain language; report compliance measures to the CAI within 90 days.
notes: CAI Surveillance section decision 1036011-S, rendered 2026-05-27 (administrative judge Me Steeven Plante). Complaint filed September 2024; notice of order issued May 20, 2025. The company had already begun corrective steps before the decision.

issue: Second phase of the Metro facial-recognition pilot investigation: whether the planned collection of personal information for a biometric characteristics bank (identifying people previously involved in shoplifting, fraud or violence across Metro, Super C and Jean Coutu banners) met the necessity test under the private-sector Act.
outcome: Collection found necessary and the planned bank not otherwise privacy-infringing; ordered Metro to report semi-annually for two years on the creation and use of the bank(s) and the effectiveness of the facial-recognition systems, including any false-positive or algorithmic-bias problems. Also recommended evaluating which sectors or regions genuinely need centralized data.
notes: CAI Surveillance section decision 1037199-S, rendered 2026-04-01 (administrative judge Me Steeven Plante). Follows the February 2025 decision prohibiting the bank under s.45 LCCJTI (no express consent); that prohibition stands and is under appeal before the Cour du Québec. This decision does not alter it.
